shopify said on stage in 2023 that 30% of its customers never finish setting up a store. we had the exact same drop-off inside autods, so we built the store for them instead. products picked from data on 400m+ listings. a million stores later that project made us shopify's biggest partner.

you budget every dollar and none of your energy. track it by the hour, a daily average hides the leak. find the block where you are always weaker and cut what sits in it. protect the evening. the hours you free up go into sleep and breathing, and whatever you stopped enjoying goes too.

every saturday i open next week's calendar and look for what to cut. an hour meeting becomes 30 minutes, 30 becomes 15. the personal development blocks never move. 3 hours a week minimum with two coaches, and my assistant knows they outrank everything. elevate yourself and the business follows.

the real scams in saas, from someone who exited at $92m. building in stealth. free users who touch every feature and never pay. a 5-year plan that stays a document forever. saying yes to every side opportunity. none of them feel like a mistake while you are inside them.

at 14 i sold e-cigarettes to my classmates in beer sheva. money upfront, delivery a month later. no connections, no investors, nobody in my family had done it. lost my ebay business after 7 years and rebuilt from zero. sold autods to fiverr at 28. whatever they say about you now means nothing.

ebay suspended my account at 21 and almost 7 years of work was gone in a day. every agent told me the suspension was final. i opened 100 accounts the next morning and built software just to run them. that black screen became autods, the company i have run for 10 years. keep going.

founders who fail wait to feel motivated, compare timelines, and push past empty. founders who win act first and let motivation follow, define what winning looks like today, take the week off before they need it, and change the part they stopped enjoying.

my playbook for a 2026 exit: build a company that runs without you, hand off anything someone does 80% as well, and know what the day after the sale looks like before signing. around 70% of owners regret selling. the game is bigger than any one company you build inside it.

A Reddit thread on founders losing old friends as the business grows had one reply worth saving. What gets outgrown is a dynamic, and the same three people are still inside it. Growth and altitude are two different things. The friends who never needed you smaller are worth the inconvenience.

cheap content is worth what it costs, and there is more of it every month. people scroll past it fast now. writing quality stopped being the check. machines already write cleaner than you do. what gets checked is whether you have done the thing, and that shows up in which details you pick.

the hacks that built a $92m saas were boring. learn the p&l of the customer you sell to. set your price off unit economics before you touch the product. hire people who can run a function without you in it. 10 years of that built a company i never set out to start.

10 companies that should exist by 2026 and still don't. ai tax filing that actually files. insurance for when your ai agent makes a costly mistake. a tutor that adapts to one kid in real time. dispatch software for plumbers with no office staff. steal one before someone else bills for it.

selling autods to fiverr for $92m was the easy part. the expensive lessons came earlier: hire the strongest people from day one and never settle, make the company profitable early and pull money out, do real tax planning before you need it. every compromise cost me years.
